pageData.title: The Toltec Empire
pageData.para1: The Toltec Empire. After Teotihuacan burned, central Mexico's next great power was the Toltecs, whose capital was Tollan-Xicocotitlan - the Tula of the Mexican chronicles - with other important cities at Tulancingo and Huapalcalco. The Toltec state existed through the Classic and Postclassic periods, gaining most of its power in the Postclassic, when its sphere of influence reached as far as the Yucatan Peninsula. The chronicles remember a theocracy founded in the year 674 that became a monarchy around 700, and the legendary priest-king Topiltzin Ce Acatl Quetzalcoatl, who ruled Tollan by the traditional account from 923 to 947 and suppressed large-scale human sacrifice. His fall unleashed a religious war between his followers and the cult of Tezcatlipoca - a conflict that flared again from 1046 to 1110 - and later a great famine (1070-1077): events that sent waves of Toltec exiles across Mesoamerica, to Uxmal and the Maya lands, where the Itza of mixed Maya-Toltec descent carried his cult as Kukulkan, and to Cholula, taken over by Toltec exiles around 1200.
pageData.para2: How much of this is history is honestly uncertain: the status of the Toltecs as an 'empire' has been disputed, and whether Tula dominated or even directly influenced the Yucatan is debated by scholars. What is certain is the Toltec legacy: the Maya city of Chichen Itza shows striking central-Mexican styles, and centuries later the Mexica remembered the Toltecs with awe - Culhuacan, the city where the Mexica first served as mercenaries, was honored as a refuge of the Toltecs - and Maya tradition carried his cult to Yucatan under the name Kukulkan. Tula was abandoned around 1122, but its warrior columns and its legend lived on in every Mexican state that claimed its inheritance.

pageData.title: Postclassic Maya (Chichén Itzá & Mayapán)
pageData.para1: The Postclassic Maya: Chichen Itza and Mayapan. When the Classic Maya cities of the south collapsed in the 9th century, Maya civilization did not die - it moved north. In the northern Yucatan, Chichen Itza rose to dominate the peninsula from the Terminal Classic into the Postclassic (c. 900-1200 AD): a city whose architecture blends Maya Puuc and Chenes styles with striking central-Mexican forms - once read as conquest from Tula, now mostly understood as cultural diffusion across a connected Maya-Mexican world. Its great pyramid, the Castillo of Kukulkan, stands over a hidden cenote never yet seen by archaeologists - the whole city sits on the buried rim of the Chicxulub impact crater, whose fractured rock feeds the sinkholes that were its water supply in a land without rivers - and its Sacred Cenote, dredged by Edward Thompson from 1904 to 1910, yielded gold, jade, pottery, incense, and human remains bearing wounds consistent with sacrifice to the rain god Chaac.
pageData.para2: As Chichen Itza declined around 1200, Mayapan inherited the leadership of the northern Maya for another two centuries, before the peninsula fragmented into rival provinces - the divided political landscape that the Spanish would later exploit. The Postclassic period in the Maya chronology runs from about 950 to the conquest era, and modern scholars treat these period divisions as conveniences of dating rather than true cultural decline. The Postclassic was the Maya world's last indigenous age: the K'iche' kingdom expanded in the Guatemalan highlands, and Maya resistance to Spain was so stubborn that the last independent Maya city, Nojpeten in the Peten lakes, fell only in 1697 - more than 170 years after the conquest began.

pageData.title: The Aztec Empire (Triple Alliance)
pageData.para1: The Aztec Empire (Triple Alliance). The last and greatest of Mexico's indigenous empires was born in 1428, when three Nahua city-states - Mexico-Tenochtitlan, Tetzcoco, and Tlacopan - formed the Triple Alliance from the victorious factions of a civil war against the city of Azcapotzalco. The Mexica of Tenochtitlan, the last of the Nahua migrants to arrive in central Mexico around 1250 - finding all the good land taken, they served as mercenaries for Culhuacan, the old refuge of the Toltecs - had founded their island city in Lake Texcoco barely a century before; within generations it was dominant over its partners and master of most of central Mexico, with outlying provinces as far as the Guatemalan border. Its people called their alliance Excān Tlahtōlōyān - we know them as the Aztec Empire.
pageData.para2: The empire ruled indirectly: conquered cities kept their rulers so long as they paid semi-annual tribute and supplied warriors, receiving protection, stability, and access to an integrated economic network in return - a hegemonic empire, not a territorial one. But it was an empire built on resentment: when Hernan Cortes landed in 1519, he found thousands of native allies eager to march against Tenochtitlan. On 13 August 1521 the city fell to the Spaniards and their indigenous allies, and its last ruler, Cuauhtemoc, became a legend of resistance. The empire the Spaniards found was sophisticated as well as mighty: Moctezuma issued laws separating nobles and commoners, and every neighborhood had a religiously supervised school - the telpochcalli for commoners, the prestigious calmecac for the nobility and future priests. The Triple Alliance had ruled the Valley of Mexico for 93 years; its fall opened all of Mesoamerica to Spain.

pageData.title: The Mixtec Civilization
pageData.para1: The Mixtec Civilization. The Mixtecs - the ñuudzahui, 'people of the rain god' - were the great civilization of the mountains and coasts of today's Oaxaca, Puebla, and Guerrero, and one of the oldest continuous cultures of Mexico: their civilization lasted from around 1500 BCE until the Spanish conquest in 1523. Their homeland, La Mixteca, was divided into three worlds: the dry highlands of the Mixteca Alta, where the region's first urbanized sites emerged; the hot Mixteca Baja; and the humid tropical Costa. Pre-Columbian Mixtec kingdoms numbered around 1.5 million people, competing and allying with each other and with their Zapotec neighbors of the Central Valleys.
pageData.para2: The Mixtecs' golden age came in the Postclassic, when the culture hero Eight Deer Jaguar Claw, from Tilantongo in the Alta, conquered kingdom after kingdom on his way down to the coast - previously the land of the Chatino people - and founded the capital of Tututepec in the Lower Rio Verde valley. Even the Baja had its own hieroglyphic script, called nuine. The Mixteca Alta has seen the most archaeological study, with evidence of settlement going back to the Archaic and Early Formative periods - some of the deepest roots of urban life in Mexico. Conquered by the Spanish and their indigenous allies in the 16th century, the Mixtec people never disappeared: about 800,000 Mixtecs live in Mexico today, with large communities in the United States as well, and their many languages remain a major branch of the Oto-Manguean family. Descended from peoples who first settled the mountains, valleys, and Pacific coast of the Mixteca in the second millennium BCE, they are one of the great surviving indigenous nations of Mesoamerica.

pageData.title: The Mississippian Culture (Cahokia)
pageData.para1: The Mississippian Culture and Cahokia. From the end of the 10th century to the 16th, the Mississippian culture transformed the river valleys of the American South and Midwest: theocratic chiefdoms, dense population centers, maize agriculture and shell-tempered pottery, the new technology of the bow and arrow, and above all the flat-topped platform mounds that crowned their towns - a leap beyond the burial mounds of the earlier Woodland peoples, crowned by a ritual world of the Corn-Mother religion and Datura ceremonies, though the Hopewell clan system endured, so that a traveler could find hospitality from a fellow clan member thousands of miles from home.
pageData.para2: Its capital was Cahokia, near today's St. Louis: founded in 1050, it was likely a planned social and religious project, and at its peak around 1124 it held at least 22,400 people - the largest city north of Mexico. The 'Cahokian Big Bang' sent missionaries and influence 500 miles north, and sites like Angel Mounds served as pilgrimage destinations; but drought and political instability after 1150 sent half its people into exile - many to the Nashville area, which peaked around 1275 - and spread Mississippian culture outward to new centers like Moundville in Alabama, the Yazoo basin, and Etowah. Around 1300 new religious ideas swept in from the west - the Datura Ritual Complex - and the Late Mississippian world organized into larger paramount chiefdoms ruled by a 'Gran Cacique,' with whole river basins emptied into 'Vacant Quarter' buffer zones between rivals. These chiefdoms were still flourishing when de Soto's expedition found them in the 1540s; within two centuries, disease and disruption had shattered the mound-building world, leaving the great mounds to puzzle the continent's newcomers.

pageData.title: The Haudenosaunee / Iroquois Confederacy
pageData.para1: The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois Confederacy). The Haudenosaunee - 'those who build the longhouse,' known to history as the Iroquois - are the great indigenous confederacy of northeastern North America: originally five nations, the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca - the Mohawk the 'Keepers of the Eastern Door' of the metaphorical longhouse, the Seneca the 'Keepers of the Western Door' - joined after 1722 by the Tuscarora as the Six Nations. Their oral history tells how the Great Peacemaker, with Hiawatha and Jigonhsasee, ended the wars between the nations and founded the confederacy under a constitution known as the Great Law of Peace - dated anywhere between 1142 and 1660 - one of the oldest continuing constitutions in the world, governing through the Grand Council.
pageData.para2: The confederacy was a superpower of the colonial-era woodlands: its unity gave the five nations military and diplomatic weight far beyond their numbers, and its matrilineal clans, longhouse religion, and wampum diplomacy made it a distinctive civilization in its own right. Armed with muskets from the fur trade, the Haudenosaunee fought the Beaver Wars and defeated or assimilated most neighboring nations; at their peak around 1700 their power reached from the lower Great Lakes south to Virginia and the Ohio Valley. For nearly 200 years they held the balance of power between the French and British colonies, aligning with Britain under the Covenant Chain. The American Revolution split the confederacy - Oneida and Tuscarora sided with the Patriots, the rest with Britain - but it never died: the Haudenosaunee reestablished their Grand Council after the war, still consider themselves sovereign, issue their own passports, and in 1923 even attempted to join the League of Nations - the oldest living experiment in federal democracy on the continent.
